title: Sector Depth Round 010 — Ten Least-Developed Sectors
method: Selected from the current European Sector Atlas by looking for sectors whose existing records remained mostly one-line research prompts rather than institution/asset/supply-chain maps. The canonical ten-level Frame is unchanged.

sectors.name: Water, Wastewater & Water Resilience
sectors.why_underdeveloped: The atlas names water as a dependency but does not yet expose the institutional, physical and financial chain that makes water a system-level input.
supply_chain: watersheds -> abstraction -> raw-water transport -> treatment -> storage -> distribution -> households/industry/agriculture -> wastewater collection -> treatment -> discharge/reuse
chemicals -> treatment plants
pumps/pipes/meters -> utilities
electricity -> pumping and treatment
construction/engineering -> network renewal
municipal finance -> capital expenditure
research_questions: Which European regions have the largest gap between available water and demand?
Where are leakage and non-revenue-water losses highest?
Which utilities depend on a small number of equipment or chemical suppliers?
Which industrial clusters compete with households or agriculture for water?
Where is wastewater reuse economically viable?
Which assets are most exposed to drought, flooding or salinity?
Who owns and finances the major water assets?
Where are renewal backlogs hidden inside municipal balance sheets?
source_leads: European Commission — European Water Resilience Strategy
European Environment Agency — water resources and resilience indicators
European Investment Bank — water investment/project database
JRC — water scarcity and drought observatories

sectors.name: Waste, Recycling & Circularity
sectors.why_underdeveloped: The repository treats waste as an output but has not yet mapped the reverse-flow economy in which discarded material becomes secondary feedstock, export, landfill or lost value.
supply_chain: consumer/industry -> collection -> sorting -> preparation -> recycling -> secondary material -> manufacturing
waste -> export/import -> foreign treatment
construction -> demolition -> aggregate/metals recovery
electronics -> collection -> dismantling -> critical-material recovery
organic waste -> anaerobic digestion/compost -> energy/soil products
research_questions: Where does each major waste stream physically go?
Which materials leave Europe rather than being recycled domestically?
Where is recycling economically constrained by low secondary-material prices?
Which European regions lack high-quality sorting or recovery capacity?
How much critical material is embedded in existing buildings, vehicles, grids and electronics?
Which producers are financially responsible for end-of-life costs?
Where could repair and refurbishment substitute for new production?
source_leads: European Commission Circular Economy Action Plan

sectors.name: Telecommunications & Connectivity
sectors.why_underdeveloped: The atlas identifies fibre and subsea cables but does not yet map operators, landing stations, backbone ownership, equipment vendors or repair capacity.
institutions: European Union Agency for the Space Programme
supply_chain: optical fibre -> cable -> terrestrial/subsea deployment -> landing station -> backbone -> exchange -> access network -> household/business
radio spectrum -> operators -> base stations -> devices
chips/electronics -> routers/switches/base stations
power -> telecom sites/data centres
subsea cable damage -> detection -> repair vessel -> replacement cable
research_questions: Who owns each major European backbone and subsea route?
Which landing stations are single points of failure?
How concentrated is European telecom equipment supply?
What is the repair-vessel capacity by sea basin?
Which cables carry both economic and strategic traffic?
Where do telecom networks depend on non-European cloud or equipment stacks?
How resilient are Arctic and North Atlantic routes?
source_leads: TeleGeography as a commercial mapping lead requiring source validation

sectors.name: Semiconductors & Electronics
sectors.why_underdeveloped: The existing node names chips and fabs but does not yet distinguish design, lithography, wafers, chemicals, fabrication, packaging, testing and downstream strategic users.
supply_chain: silica/silicon -> polysilicon -> wafers -> fabrication -> packaging -> testing -> electronics assembly -> automotive/industrial/defence/cloud
specialty chemicals -> fabs
lithography/equipment -> fabs
electricity + ultrapure water -> fabs
EDA software/IP -> chip design
research_questions: Which chip categories are actually fabricated in Europe?
Where are Europe's largest single-source dependencies?
Which fabs are strategically important and who controls them?
Where is advanced packaging capacity located?
How dependent are European firms on non-European EDA tools and IP?
Which water and electricity systems are critical to fabs?
Which European chip capabilities could be expanded fastest?

sectors.name: Cloud, Data Centres & Compute
sectors.why_underdeveloped: The repository recognises compute but has not yet treated data centres as physical infrastructure requiring land, electricity, cooling, fibre, chips, financing and grid capacity.
supply_chain: land/building -> grid connection -> transformers/substation -> cooling -> servers -> chips -> fibre -> cloud platform -> enterprise/public users
electricity -> compute -> heat -> cooling -> water/air systems
capital -> data-centre construction -> long-term contracted revenue
research_questions: Where is European compute physically located?
Who owns the buildings, servers and cloud platforms?
How much grid capacity is reserved for data centres?
Which regions face water stress from cooling demand?
What share of strategic workloads depends on non-European hyperscalers?
Where can waste heat be reused?
Which data centres have independent power or backup generation?
source_leads: European Commission Digital Decade and cloud policy

sectors.name: Insurance & Pensions
sectors.why_underdeveloped: The repository has obligations and finance but barely exposes the institutional owners of Europe's long-duration capital and risk-bearing capacity.
supply_chain: households/employers -> contributions/premiums -> insurers/pension funds -> capital markets -> bonds/equities/infrastructure/real estate -> returns -> pensions/claims
risk -> insurance -> reinsurance -> global capital
demography -> liabilities -> required assets -> investment strategy
research_questions: Who ultimately owns European infrastructure through pension and insurance capital?
What proportion of pension assets is invested domestically?
How exposed are insurers to sovereign debt and real estate?
Where do demographic changes create asset-liability stress?
Which infrastructure projects could match long-duration liabilities?
How much European capital is managed by non-European firms?

sectors.name: Public Administration & Government Services
sectors.why_underdeveloped: The tree names institutions, laws and public finance but does not expose the machinery between legislation, budgets and actual service delivery.
supply_chain: constitution/law -> ministry/agency -> budget appropriation -> procurement -> contractor -> service -> citizen/business -> measurement/audit
tax base -> collection -> treasury -> transfers/services -> households/firms
public data -> registers -> digital services -> policy evaluation
research_questions: Which functions are duplicated across ministries, agencies and levels of government?
Where does procurement concentrate spending among a small supplier set?
Which public registers are foundational infrastructure?
How much administrative capacity is consumed by compliance versus service delivery?
Where are digital systems interoperable or fragmented?
Which government assets are underused or duplicated?
Can service outcomes be mapped against staffing and expenditure?
source_leads: Eurostat government finance and employment data
European Commission digital-government and public-administration programmes

sectors.name: Media, Culture & Information
sectors.why_underdeveloped: The repository treats information as an output but does not map the physical, financial and institutional systems through which information is produced, distributed, archived and monetised.
supply_chain: reporting/research -> newsroom -> editing -> rights clearance -> publication -> platform/broadcast distribution -> audience -> advertising/subscription/public funding
cultural production -> rights ownership -> licensing -> distribution -> royalties
archives -> digitisation -> searchable public/private information
research_questions: Who owns the major European news and media groups?
Which platforms control distribution rather than production?
How much public information depends on private platforms?
Where are archives privately owned or at risk of disappearing?
How are public-service media financed?
What are the largest cross-border information flows?
Which dependencies create information bottlenecks during crises?
source_leads: European Commission European Media Freedom Act materials

sectors.name: Maritime, Ports & Shipbuilding
sectors.why_underdeveloped: The repository recognises ports and shipping but does not yet map the asset chain connecting harbours, shipyards, fleets, cargo, offshore energy, cables and repair capacity.
institutions: European Maritime Transport Environmental Report partners
supply_chain: shipyard -> steel/engines/electronics -> vessel -> port -> cargo terminal -> rail/road -> industrial/consumer market
offshore wind -> installation vessels -> ports -> turbines/cables -> grid
subsea cable -> cable ship -> landing station -> telecom/energy network
port -> customs -> logistics -> manufacturing/retail
research_questions: Which North Sea and North Atlantic ports are systemically important?
Who owns the major ports and terminals?
Where is European shipbuilding and repair capacity located?
How many specialised cable and offshore vessels exist?
Which ports can support offshore-wind expansion?
Where do rail/road connections bottleneck port throughput?
Which ports combine energy, trade and security functions?
source_leads: European Commission TEN-T and Motorways of the Sea

sectors.name: Nuclear Energy & Fuel Cycle
sectors.why_underdeveloped: Nuclear exists as a node but the repository does not yet expose the fuel cycle, reactor fleet, engineering base, regulation, waste chain or ownership structure.
supply_chain: uranium mining -> conversion -> enrichment -> fuel fabrication -> reactor -> spent fuel -> storage -> reprocessing/disposal
nuclear engineering -> reactor components -> construction/maintenance
reactor -> electricity grid
research reactors -> medical/industrial isotopes
research_questions: Which parts of Europe's fuel cycle are domestic, allied or externally dependent?
Who owns the operating reactor fleet?
Which components have single-source suppliers?
Where are the largest engineering and maintenance capabilities?
What is the status of national spent-fuel and geological-disposal programmes?
Which reactors provide medical isotopes or other non-electricity outputs?
What grid and financing constraints govern new nuclear construction?

cross_sector_edges_to_add.why: Fabs require large volumes of highly purified water.
Compute expansion is physically constrained by grid connection and power availability.
Cloud capacity is only useful at scale when connected through resilient fibre and exchange infrastructure.
Secondary materials can substitute for some primary extraction and create domestic material flows.
Long-duration liabilities can hold long-duration infrastructure assets and debt.
Government procurement is a cross-sector demand mechanism and a potential industrial-policy lever.
Offshore energy, subsea cables and heavy components depend on ports and specialised vessels.
Nuclear provides dispatchable low-carbon electricity and specialised industrial capabilities.
Modern information distribution is physically carried by communications networks.
Compute capacity ultimately requires processors, memory, networking and power electronics.

epistemic_rule: Institution and asset names are source leads, not claims of ownership or control. Ownership, capacity, dependency and financial relationships must be verified entity-by-entity from primary or high-quality institutional sources before promotion into the core graph.
